Remaining peoples complicate the conquest account

The chapter starts with victories and ends with a list of failures. Verses 27–33 repeat one phrase for five tribes: they “didn’t drive out” the people. Verse 28 adds what Israel did when it was strong enough to finish. It chose forced labor over the command. In verse 34 the Amorites even push Dan into the hills. Chapter 2:1–3 gives the LORD’s response to this.
A generation change becomes a problem of memory

Verse 7 says Israel served the LORD while people lived who “had seen” his work. Verse 10 says the next generation “didn’t know the LORD” or what he had done. The text does not say they were told and refused. It says they did not know. Deuteronomy 6:7 and Joshua 4:6–7 had ordered parents to tell the story. Verses 11–19 then lay out the cycle the book will repeat. The trouble begins as a failure of memory between parents and children.
Deliverance uses an unexpected advantage

Verse 15 calls Ehud “a left-handed man” before he does anything. The detail explains the plan. Ehud straps his sword on the right thigh, under his clothes (verse 16). That is not the side where one would look for a weapon. He draws it with his left hand (verse 21). The text treats a trait that set him apart as the means of rescue. Each rescue in this chapter begins the same way: Israel “cried to the LORD.”
Victory disrupts expected roles

Deborah holds two roles in verse 4: prophetess and judge. Barak is the general, yet he will not march without her (verse 8). Verse 9 says the cost: the honor will go to “a woman.” A reader might expect that woman to be Deborah. Verses 17–21 give the victory to Jael, a tent dweller and not an Israelite. Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots and dies by a tent peg. The chapter credits God with the result (verse 23).
A victory song also judges participation

The song praises God and also keeps a record of who came. Verses 14–15 and 18 name tribes that risked their lives. Verses 16–17 name those that did not: Reuben, Gilead, Dan, and Asher. Each is pictured at its ordinary work, with flocks or ships. The poem asks them why and gives no excuse. Verse 23 curses a town that would not help. The poem closes with an enemy’s mother waiting, and it lets the reader see her.
The first conflict occurs inside Gideon's household

Gideon’s first task is at home, not on a battlefield. The Baal altar belongs to his own father (verse 25). He does it at night because he fears his family and the town (verse 27). The town demands his death. In verse 31 his father, the altar’s owner, defends him. His argument is simple: a real god can fight for himself. So the first person won over is inside Gideon’s household.
Reduced numbers change the explanation of victory

Armies want more soldiers, and the LORD orders fewer. Verse 2 gives the reason before the cuts begin. With a large force Israel would say its own hand had saved it. So the number drops from thousands to three hundred (verses 3–7). Their gear is trumpets, jars, and torches, not swords in hand (verse 16). Verse 22 says the LORD turned the enemy’s swords on each other. The size of the army is set so the credit cannot be mistaken.
A deliverer's achievement can produce another danger

Gideon began by tearing down an idol’s altar (6:27). In verse 23 he refuses to be king and says the LORD will rule. His very next act is to ask for gold (verse 24). He makes an ephod, a priestly object, and sets it up in his town. Verse 27 says all Israel went after it and it became “a snare.” Aaron also made an idol from gold earrings (Exodus 32:2–4). The deliverer leaves behind a new thing for Israel to worship.
The tree story examines consent to dangerous rule

In Jotham’s story the useful trees refuse to rule. Each has oil, fruit, or wine to give and will not leave it. Only the bramble says yes. A bramble has no real shade to offer, and it burns easily. Its speech in verse 15 offers “refuge” and threatens fire in the same breath. Jotham applies it to Shechem: they chose a killer as king (verses 16–20). Verses 49 and 57 report that fire did come on Shechem.
Confession cannot function as a quick transaction

Israel’s first confession in verse 10 is quick. The LORD’s answer in verses 11–14 is a refusal. He has rescued them many times, and each time they left. Verse 14 tells them to ask their chosen gods for help. The second confession adds two things (verses 15–16). They accept whatever God decides, and they put the foreign gods away. Only then does the text say his soul was grieved for their misery.
A vow can expose failed judgment

The LORD’s Spirit is already on Jephthah in verse 29. He still adds a vow in verses 30–31, as if a bargain were needed. The vow is loose: “whatever comes out” of his door. His daughter comes out, as women did to greet victors (Exodus 15:20). In verse 35 he says she has brought him low. The words put the weight on her, though the vow was his. The text never says God asked for this vow or approved it.
A speech difference becomes a weapon

Ephraim made the same complaint to Gideon in 8:1. Gideon answered softly, and the anger passed. Jephthah answers with a charge and then with war (verses 2–4). The test at the river in verse 6 uses one word. A small difference in speech marks a man as the enemy. These are Israelites killing Israelites, tribe against tribe. The count in verse 6 is forty-two thousand of their own people.
The mother interprets the encounter more clearly

The angel comes to the woman both times, not to Manoah (verses 3 and 9). She is never named, yet she receives the message and the rules. Manoah asks for a repeat and then for the angel’s name. In verse 22 he concludes they will die. His wife answers with three plain reasons in verse 23. God took their offering, showed them these things, and told them of a son. She reads the event correctly while her husband panics.
A contest exposes someone with less power

The riddle is a contest between Samson and thirty men. In verse 15 the men turn on the one person outside the bet. They threaten to burn the bride and her father’s house. She has no protector, since her husband is on the other side. She weeps for seven days until he tells her (verse 17). Samson then blames her in verse 18. In 15:6 the Philistines burn her and her father anyway.
Retaliation spreads beyond its original dispute

Each side in this chapter says it is only paying back. Samson says so in verses 3 and 7, and the Philistines in verse 10. In verse 11 Samson says he did to them as they did to him. The first victims in verse 6 are the woman and her father. They are burned for a wrong done to them, not by them. Judah’s men then side with their rulers against Samson (verse 11). No one in the chapter stops the chain; it only grows.
The final victory comes after loss of control

Until now Samson has acted by his own strength and for his own reasons. In verse 20 he does not know the LORD has left him. The Philistines take his eyes, which led him from the start (14:1). Verse 28 is only his second recorded prayer (15:18 is the first). He asks to be remembered and strengthened “only this once.” His stated reason is still personal: revenge for his two eyes. Verse 30 says he killed more in his death than in his life.
Religious hiring becomes a claim to security

Micah’s religion mixes the LORD’s name with things the law forbids. His mother dedicates silver “to the LORD” for a carved image (verse 3). He owns a private shrine and appoints his own priest (verse 5). Hiring a real Levite seems to him to fix everything. Verse 13 shows his reasoning: a proper priest guarantees God’s favor. Verse 6 gives the writer’s comment on the whole scene. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
Migration carries theft into a new sanctuary

Micah stole from his mother in 17:2. Now armed men steal from him. His cry in verse 24 is honest about his gods: “which I made.” A god that can be made can also be carried off. The priest goes with the stronger party without protest (verse 20). Verse 27 calls the people of Laish “quiet and unsuspecting” when Dan kills them. Verse 30 traces the new shrine’s priests to a grandson of Moses.
The final violence reaches inside Israel

The travelers pass Jebus because it is not an Israelite town (verse 12). They expect safety among their own people in Gibeah. What happens there copies Sodom in Genesis 19. This time no angel steps in, and the woman is handed out. The Levite who gave her up is the one who reports the crime. Verse 30 says nothing like it had been seen since Egypt. The woman is never named and never speaks.
The assembly acts on a selective report

The assembly hears one witness, the Levite (verses 4–6). He says the men of Gibeah meant to kill him. He does not say he put the woman outside himself (19:25). On that account he asks all Israel for a verdict (verse 7). The tribes swear to act before anyone questions him. Benjamin’s refusal in verse 13 then turns a trial into a war. By verse 48 Israel is burning Benjamin’s towns and killing all in them.
A proposed repair repeats harm against women

Israel made two oaths in anger and now feels trapped (verses 1 and 5). The leaders look for ways around their own words. One oath is kept by destroying Jabesh Gilead (verses 10–11). The other is dodged by letting women be taken, not “given” (verse 22). The elders prepare a legal excuse for the fathers in advance. No one asks the women of Jabesh or Shiloh. The last verse judges all of it: everyone did what seemed right.
